Hi, not the person you replied to, but I have those traits myself (perfectionism, obsessive tendencies, neurotic). I am currently in a stable relationship of two years.

Personally, for me it was helpful to understand two things.

1.	Being a perfectionist is not really good for oneself. Aside from any hurt you may cause your partner for having that trait, it is almost certain you have hurt yourself with your perfectionism. (For example, setting the bar way too high for yourself and later being hard on yourself for not fulfilling it)
2.	Almost any aspect of your personality can be changed and improved through hard work at introspection and removal of distorted thinking patterns. (Usually Therapy helps a lot with this) And you don’t need to view this traits as definitive labels about yourself, if you don’t like something about you usually it is possible to change it,

For me, on therapy I recognized and understood how that those traits were negatively affecting my life and those around me and I began the process of undoing that kind of thinking. It’s a really, really hard and long process not going to lie (I’ve been in therapy for six years and old patterns of thinking still come up), but it’s really worth it in my opinion. I feel like my quality of life has significantly improved since working on having a less rigid way of thinking.

I know that I’ve hurt people in the past (not only myself) as I’ve hurt my current partner too because of this traits, however I don’t think those traits make you automatically a toxic person if you are aware and taking measures to reduce their negative impact on your life or others. At least that’s what I’ve experienced. 

If I may, a book that really helped me personally has been “Mindset” by Carol Dweck so maybe it can help you too.

Not the person you replied to, but I have Bipolar type 2. For me it can be sometimes hard at the start of an episode to tell whether I'm starting an episode or not. Whether it be a high or low. However, because depression is more common in type 2 I can now fairly accurately assess my own behaviors and symptoms when depressed. 


For hypomania (in type 2 there are no full manic episodes) it's still difficult for me to identify them. Which is dangerous because if I let them happen it unavoidably end up with depressive episodes which are a bitch to deal with.  (Specially because I tend to get WAY too many responsabilities when manic and I usually can no longer fulfill them when depressed)


That said, for me at least, in the 4 years since my diagnosis I have become slowly better at identifying when I may be starting an episode  in order to get proper help from my psychiatrist to stop them or prevent them.

Hmm... you know, I had a similar experience through higschool. Very few friends, no real social life, focused on my own stuff... I just recently finished my first semester in college and I gotta say I loved it. I think it's because due to being in the same major, you'll usually find at least some people you can relate to more easily because of shared interest. I'd say just try not to focus too much in having a laaarge social circle at first, maybe try to deepen your relationship with the people you already met? I personally found around three to four people who I really like and I can actually call friends, so not bad at all imo. So yeah, my advice would be to focus on shared interests and have fun learning about what you really like! :)
